usage: Standard polite question to any shopkeeper
반말, only to a friend or younger seller you know
Formal 합쇼체, stiff but very polite
Asking the total for several items
examples: 이거 얼마예요?
How much is this?
Bare question while pointing at one item — the most common form
A: 사장님, 이 사과 한 봉지에 얼마예요? / B: 오천 원이에요.
A: Boss, how much for a bag of apples? / B: Five thousand won.
사장님 is the polite way to address any shop owner; shows full exchange at a market stall
저기요, 이 가방 색깔별로 가격이 달라요? 검은색은 얼마예요?
Excuse me, are the prices different by color? How much is the black one?
저기요 gets attention first; 색깔별로 = by color — a more complex real-world use
nuance: 얼마예요? is the single most useful shopping phrase: 얼마 means 'how much/how many' and 예요 is the polite copula ('is it'), so it literally asks 'it is how much?'. It sits at everyday 해요체, perfectly polite for markets, shops, and taxis, and is the blunt, direct market question you deploy the moment you want a number right now. Drop to 얼마야? only with a friend; rise to 얼마입니까? at a formal counter or on the phone. The nearest alternative, 가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what's the price?'), is softer and more common when asking for a quote or service estimate, while 얼마예요? is the in-hand item question. The classic English-speaker spelling error is 얼마에요 — after a noun ending in a vowel the copula is -예요, not -에요; the over-spelled 얼마이에요 is also wrong.

structuredNuance.t: 얼마 = 'how much/many' + 예요 = polite copula 'is it'. Literally 'it is how much?' — a complete, natural price question in one breath.

해요체 — suitable for any shop owner, market vendor, or taxi driver you don't know personally. Drop to 얼마야? with friends; 얼마입니까? at formal counters. Use whenever you want a number immediately after seeing an item.

가격이 어떻게 돼요? ('what is the price?') is softer and fits asking for an estimate or service quote. The dividing line: 얼마예요? targets a specific item in hand and expects a number now; 가격이 어떻게 돼요? is more open-ended.
다 해서 얼마예요? (total for everything), 한 개에 얼마예요? (price per piece), 원래 얼마예요? (original price?). All follow the same 얼마예요 base.

Spelling it 얼마에요 is the #1 error — after a vowel-ending noun the copula must be 예요, not 에요. 얼마이에요 is over-spelled and unnatural. Never say 얼마 비싸요? ('how expensive?') — that is not how Korean asks price.

mistakes: Spelling it 얼마에요.
After a noun ending in a vowel the polite copula is -예요, not -에요. The correct, natural spelling is 얼마예요?
Asking 얼마 많아요? thinking 많다 means 'much'.
많다 is 'many/a lot' (quantity), not price. Price uses the fixed word 얼마, so it is 얼마예요?
Using 얼마야? with a shop clerk you don't know.
얼마야? is 반말 and sounds rude to a stranger. To any seller use 얼마예요? or 얼마입니까?

usage: Pointing at one item near you, polite
반말 to a friend running a stall
Formal 합쇼체, 이것은 is the full written form
저거 = that thing over there, out of reach
examples: 이거 얼마예요?
How much is this?
Touching or pointing at the item as you ask — most minimal, most common form
A: 이거 얼마예요? / B: 이만 원이에요. / A: 좀 깎아 주세요.
A: How much is this? / B: Twenty thousand won. / A: Give me a discount, please.
Full market exchange showing how price-asking leads naturally into haggling
이거 얼마예요? 아, 생각보다 비싸네요. 좀 더 둘러볼게요.
How much is this? Oh, pricier than I thought. I'll look around a bit more.
Polite exit after hearing the price; 생각보다 = more than expected; 둘러볼게요 = I'll browse
nuance: 이거 얼마예요? is the pointing version of the price question, used when the item is right in front of you or in your hand; 이거 is the spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing'), so it means 'this — how much?'. Compared to bare 얼마예요?, adding 이거 removes all ambiguity when several items sit side by side. The three-way distance system — 이거 (near me) / 그거 (near you) / 저거 (far from both) — is lost on English speakers who only have 'this/that', so 그거 and 저거 are constantly mixed up. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이거 얼마야?, formal 이것은 얼마입니까?. In speech, Koreans almost always use the contracted 이거, not the full 이것; and no particle is attached (not 이거가/이거를) before 얼마예요.

structuredNuance.t: 이거 = spoken contraction of 이것 ('this thing') + 얼마예요? = 'is it how much?'. Whole meaning: 'this thing here — how much is it?' The 이거 pins the question to one specific visible item.
해요체 — use with any vendor or clerk while pointing at or holding an item. Casual 이거 얼마야? with a friend. 이것은 얼마입니까? in a formal showroom or on a price-query call.

Bare 얼마예요? with a gesture works too, but 이거 얼마예요? is unambiguous when multiple items are nearby. 이거 vs 그거 vs 저거: 이거 = near speaker; 그거 = near listener; 저거 = far from both. Mixing 그거 and 저거 is the #1 distance error.
그거 얼마예요? (that one near you), 저거 얼마예요? (that one over there), 이거 두 개에 얼마예요? (two of these). All swap only the demonstrative.
Saying 이것 얼마예요? in speech — in conversation Koreans almost always shorten 이것 to 이거. Adding a particle (이거를 얼마예요?) is also wrong; 얼마예요? takes no object particle.

mistakes: Saying 이것 얼마예요? in conversation.
이것 is the written form; spoken Korean contracts it to 이거. Natural speech is 이거 얼마예요?
Adding a particle: 이거를 얼마예요?
얼마예요 takes no object; the thing is simply named as the topic. Say 이거 얼마예요? with no 를/가.
Using 저거 for an item right in your hand.
저거 means 'that, far away'. For something you're holding use 이거. Pick the right distance word.

usage: Please knock the price down a bit
반말 to a friend or familiar vendor
Couldn't you take just a little off?
If you take some off, I'll buy right away
Offering to close the deal as leverage
examples: 좀 깎아 주세요.
Please give me a discount.
Bare haggle line at a traditional market stall — say this while holding the item
A: 두 개 살게요. 좀 깎아 주세요. / B: 그럼 오백 원 드릴게요.
A: I'll take two. Give me a bit off. / B: Okay, I'll take five hundred won off.
Volume as a bargaining chip — classic market exchange showing a realistic seller response
현금으로 낼게요. 만 원만 깎아 주세요.
I'll pay cash. Take off just 10,000 won, please.
Cash offer as leverage; 만 원만 = just 10,000 won; 현금 = cash
nuance: 좀 깎아 주세요 is a customer's haggling request, appropriate only where bargaining is culturally normal — traditional markets (시장), street stalls, some electronics alleys — but emphatically NOT in department stores, franchises, or convenience stores, where it will just embarrass everyone. 깎다 literally means 'to shave or whittle down', so you ask the seller to 'shave a bit off the quoted price'; 좀 ('a little') is the essential softener that makes it a polite request rather than a blunt demand, and -아 주세요 means 'please do it for me'. It sits at polite 해요체; drop to 깎아 줘 only with a friend; soften up to 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? for a more pleading tone. The nearest alternative, 싸게 해 주세요, asks for a lower price in general, while 깎아 주세요 specifically acts on an already-stated number — the dividing line is that 깎다 cuts from a concrete price you just heard. English speakers reach for 디스카운트 or 할인해 주세요, but 할인 is a store-set promotion, not something customers demand by hand; the market verb is 깎다.

structuredNuance.t: 깎다 = 'to shave/whittle down' + 주세요 = 'please do for me'. Literally 'please shave (the price) down a bit for me.' The image is of shaving a lump of price off, not applying a percentage discount.

해요체 — use at traditional markets (시장), street stalls, or electronics alleys where haggling is expected. NEVER in department stores, branded shops, or convenience stores — it falls flat and embarrasses the clerk. The vendor must have already said a price before 깎아 주세요 makes sense.

싸게 해 주세요 ('make it cheaper') is a softer, more general request not tied to a specific quoted number. 조금만 깎아 주시면 안 돼요? is more pleading and deferential. 깎아 주시면 바로 살게요 adds the incentive of an immediate purchase.
오천 원만 깎아 주세요 (take off just 5,000 won), 조금만 깎아 주세요 (just a tiny bit), 많이 깎아 주세요 (a lot off). Insert 조금만/얼마만/많이 to calibrate the ask.
Saying 디스카운트 주세요 or 할인해 주세요 at a market sounds off — 할인 is a store's own promotional pricing, not a face-to-face haggle. Dropping 좀 (saying just 깎아 주세요) sounds blunt, almost like an order.

mistakes: Saying 디스카운트 주세요 or 할인해 주세요 to haggle.
할인 is a store-set sale, not something you request face to face; the loanword sounds off. The market verb is 깎다: 좀 깎아 주세요.
Dropping 좀 and just saying 깎아 주세요 flatly.
Without 좀 it sounds blunt, almost like an order. 좀 softens it into a polite request, so include it.
Trying to haggle in a department store or chain.
깎아 주세요 only works where bargaining is expected (markets, stalls). In fixed-price shops it just confuses the clerk.

usage: Polite reaction to a high price
반말 muttered to a companion or friend
Softer, indirect — gentler than a flat 비싸요
examples: 너무 비싸요.
It's too expensive.
Bare reaction right after hearing the price — can double as an opener to haggling
A: 오만 원이에요. / B: 너무 비싸요. 좀 깎아 주세요.
A: It's fifty thousand won. / B: That's too expensive. Give me a discount, please.
Classic market exchange — reacting to price and immediately pivoting to haggling
디자인은 마음에 드는데 너무 비싸요. 좀 더 생각해 볼게요.
I like the design, but it's too expensive. I'll think about it more.
Polite exit strategy; -는데 = 'but'; 생각해 볼게요 = I'll think about it
nuance: 너무 비싸요 is a customer's direct reaction to a price that feels too high, said either to the seller (as an opener to haggling) or muttered to a friend; 비싸다 means 'to be expensive' and 너무 means 'too/excessively', so 'it's too expensive'. Said to a seller at a market it is practically the first move of negotiation. Politeness is 해요체; with friends it becomes 너무 비싸 (반말). To sound less blunt — avoiding offense to the goods or the seller — Koreans soften to 좀 비싼 것 같아요 ('it seems a bit pricey'), which adds hedging distance. The most confusing pair is 비싸다 vs 싸다 (cheap); do not confuse 싸다 ('cheap') with 사다 ('to buy') — they romanize the same but are entirely different verbs. English speakers often treat 너무 like 'very', as in 너무 좋아요 ('I love it so much'), but classically 너무 carries a negative 'excessively' edge that fits 너무 비싸요; for pure praise prefer 정말/아주. Spelling: 비싸요, never 비싸여요.

structuredNuance.t: 너무 = 'too/excessively' + 비싸다 = 'to be expensive'. Literally 'it is excessively expensive.' The 너무 signals that the price crosses a line — it's not just pricey, it's over your limit.

해요체 — say to any seller after hearing a price. Said to a vendor it functions as the opening move of haggling; said to a friend beside you it's a shared complaint. Soften to 좀 비싼 것 같아요 if you don't want to offend. 반말 form 너무 비싸 for friends only.

좀 비싼 것 같아요 is indirect and tentative — 'it seems a bit pricey' — so you don't insult the seller's goods. 생각보다 비싸네요 ('pricier than I expected') adds surprise without being confrontational. The dividing line: 너무 비싸요 is direct and slightly negative; the others hedge.
꽤 비싸요 (quite expensive), 많이 비싸요 (very expensive), 좀 비싸네요 (a bit pricey, with -네요 expressing mild surprise). Each step down reduces directness.

English speakers use 너무 as a neutral intensifier like 'very', but in careful Korean 너무 still carries a faintly negative 'excessive' edge. Spelling: 비싸요 not 비싸여요 (비싸다 is already 비싸 + 요). Also beware: 싸다 = cheap, 사다 = buy — same romanization, opposite meanings.

mistakes: Confusing 비싸다 (expensive) with 싸다 (cheap).
They are opposites. 비싸다 = expensive, 싸다 = cheap. Saying 너무 싸요 means 'it's too cheap', the reverse complaint.
Writing 너무 비싸여요.
비싸다's polite form is 비싸 + 요 = 비싸요, no extra 여. The correct form is 너무 비싸요.
Mixing up 싸다 (cheap) and 사다 (buy).
Different verbs that romanize alike. 싸다 = be cheap, 사다 = to buy. Context and spelling keep them apart.

usage: Polite request to a clothing clerk
반말 to a friend shopping with you
Would it be okay to try it on?
Stating intent after getting the okay
examples: 이거 입어 봐도 돼요?
Can I try this on?
Bare request while holding a garment — the most common phrasing
이 셔츠 입어 봐도 돼요? 탈의실 어디예요?
Can I try this shirt on? Where's the fitting room?
Natural follow-up; 탈의실 = fitting room — two questions in the right order
A: 사이즈가 애매해서요, 입어 봐도 돼요? M이랑 L 둘 다 볼게요. / B: 네, 탈의실은 저쪽이에요.
A: The size is borderline, so can I try it on? I'll check both M and L. / B: Sure, the fitting room is over there.
Real sizing dilemma; 애매하다 = borderline/unclear — shows full clerk interaction
nuance: 입어 봐도 돼요? is a customer asking a clothing clerk for permission to try a garment on; it is built from 입다 ('to wear') + -아/어 보다 ('try doing') + -아도 돼요? ('is it okay to?'), so literally 'is it okay if I try wearing it?'. The critical point for English speakers: Korean splits 'wear' strictly by body part — 입다 for clothes on the torso and legs (shirts, trousers, dresses), 신다 for shoes and socks, 쓰다 for hats and glasses, 끼다 for gloves and rings. Using 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes will confuse a clerk. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 입어 봐도 될까요? for extra deference; casual is 입어 봐도 돼?. The nearest alternative, 한번 봐도 돼요? ('can I take a look?'), only asks to look, not to put on — 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically requests to wear it.

structuredNuance.t: 입다 (to wear) + -어 보다 (try doing) + -아도 돼요? (is it okay to?). Literally: 'is it okay if I try wearing it?' The -어 보다 component is what encodes 'try' — without it, 입어도 돼요? merely asks 'can I wear it?', not 'can I try it on for fit?'.

해요체 — say to any clothing clerk when holding a garment and wanting to test the fit. Soften to 입어 봐도 될까요? for extra politeness (e.g., a high-end boutique). Use only for clothes (입다), not for shoes (신어 봐도 돼요?) or hats (써 봐도 돼요?).
한번 봐도 돼요? ('can I take a look?') only requests visual inspection. 입어 봐도 돼요? specifically asks to put it on. After permission, follow with 탈의실 어디예요? (where is the fitting room?).
신어 봐도 돼요? (shoes), 써 봐도 돼요? (hats/glasses), 끼어 봐도 돼요? (gloves/rings), 한번 입어 볼게요 (I'll try it on). Match the verb to the body part.
Saying 시도해 봐도 돼요? (시도하다 = 'to attempt') is wrong — that verb is for tasks, not clothing. Using 입어 for shoes is the most common error. And write 돼요, not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼).

mistakes: Using 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes.
입다 is for clothing on the body, not feet. Shoes take 신다, so for shoes ask 신어 봐도 돼요?
Saying 시도해 봐도 돼요? for 'try on'.
시도하다 means 'to attempt' (an action), not to try clothing. The fitting-room verb is 입어 보다: 입어 봐도 돼요?
Writing 입어 봐도 되요?
The polite form of 되다 here is 돼요 (되 + 어요), not 되요. Correct: 입어 봐도 돼요?

usage: Polite request in a shoe shop
Would it be okay to try them on?
한 사이즈 큰 거 신어 볼게요
Asking to test the next size
examples: 이거 신어 봐도 돼요?
Can I try these on?
Bare request pointing at a shoe on display — the most common opening line in a shoe shop
이 운동화 신어 봐도 돼요? 250 사이즈로요.
Can I try these sneakers on? In size 250.
Korean shoe sizes are in mm — 250 = 25.0 cm foot length; always state in mm
A: 발이 좀 넓어서요, 신어 봐도 돼요? / B: 네, 이쪽으로 앉으세요. / A: 좀 끼면 한 치수 큰 거 볼게요.
A: My feet are a bit wide, can I try them on? / B: Yes, please sit here. / A: If they pinch I'll check a size up.
Real fitting room exchange; 끼다 = to feel tight; 치수 = size step
nuance: 신어 봐도 돼요? is the shoe-shop counterpart of 입어 봐도 돼요?: a customer asks to try footwear on. 신다 is the verb specifically for putting on shoes, socks, and boots (things on your feet), combined with -어 보다 ('try') and -아도 돼요? ('may I?'), giving 'may I try putting them on?'. The body-part split is non-negotiable: 신다 for footwear, never 입다, and confusing them sounds bizarre to a native clerk. Politeness is 해요체; soften to 신어 봐도 될까요?; casual 신어 봐도 돼?. Korean shoe sizes are stated in millimeters (250, 255, 260, 265…), which surprises foreigners used to UK/US number sizing, so you'll always pair this phrase with a size: 250 사이즈로요. The nearest generic alternative, 한번 봐도 돼요? (just to look), only asks to examine, not to put on. Spelling: 신어 comes from 신다 + 어 — the stem vowel ㅣ takes 어, not 아.

structuredNuance.t: 신다 (to put on footwear) + -어 보다 (try doing) + -아도 돼요? (is it okay to?). Literally 'is it okay if I try putting them on?' 신다 is the body-part-specific verb for feet — shoes, socks, and boots only.
해요체 — use with any shoe shop clerk. Soften to 신어 봐도 될까요? for deference. Casual 신어 봐도 돼? with a friend. Korean shoe sizes run in mm (250, 255, 260…), so state the size as a number in millimeters.
한번 봐도 돼요? only asks to look. 입어 봐도 돼요? is for clothing on the body — using it for shoes sounds strange. The verb must match the body part.
다른 색 신어 봐도 돼요? (try another color), 한 치수 큰 거 신어 볼게요 (I'll try a size up), 더 큰 거 있어요? (do you have bigger?). All build on the same 신어 보다 core.

Saying 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes — English has one word 'wear' for everything, but Korean demands 신다 for feet. Giving a US/UK shoe size ('8' or '9') — say the mm number instead (250, 260). Spelling: 신어 봐도, not 신아 봐도 (stem ㅣ → 어).

mistakes: Saying 입어 봐도 돼요? for shoes.
입다 is for clothes on the body. Footwear uses 신다, so the shoe-shop phrase is 신어 봐도 돼요?
Giving a US/UK shoe size like '8' or '9'.
Korean shoes are sized in millimeters (250, 255, 260...). Say a mm number, e.g., 250 사이즈로요.
Writing 신아 봐도 돼요?
신다 + 어 = 신어 (the stem vowel ㅣ takes 어, not 아). Correct: 신어 봐도 돼요?

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar seller
Do you have it in black?
Naming the exact color you want
examples: 이거 다른 색 있어요?
Do you have this in another color?
Bare request holding one item — most natural opening in a clothing shop
이 가방 다른 색 있어요? 흰색은 좀 부담스러워서요.
Do you have this bag in another color? White feels a bit much for me.
Giving a reason; 부담스럽다 = feels overwhelming or too much
A: 이 코트 마음에 드는데 다른 색 있어요? / B: 네이비랑 베이지 있어요. / A: 베이지로 볼게요.
A: I like this coat — do you have other colors? / B: We have navy and beige. / A: I'll check the beige one.
Full color consultation; 네이비/베이지 are common loanword color names
nuance: 다른 색 있어요? is a customer asking a clerk whether an item comes in a different color; 다른 means 'other/different', 색 is the short spoken form of 색깔 ('color'), and 있어요? is the availability question 'is there / do you have?'. Politeness is everyday 해요체; casual 다른 색 있어?, softer 다른 색깔도 있나요?. The verb of stock/availability is always 있다 ('to exist/have') — Korean has no separate 'have' verb for this, which trips beginners who hunt for one. To name a specific color you want, use COLOR + 으로/로 있어요? e.g., 검은색으로 있어요? The critical pair to watch is 다른 ('other/different') vs 다음 ('next') — 다음 색 would mean 'next color', which is nonsensical. The nearest alternative, 다른 거 있어요? ('do you have a different one?'), asks for a different item in general, while 다른 색 있어요? pins the question specifically to color.

structuredNuance.t: 다른 = 'other/different' + 색 = short for 색깔 'color' + 있어요? = 'is there/do you have?'. Literally 'is there a different color?' Korean availability questions use 있다, not a separate 'have' verb.
해요체 — use with any clerk while holding the item you like but want in another shade. Casual 다른 색 있어? with a friend. To name the color you want: COLOR + 으로 있어요? (예: 검은색으로 있어요?).
다른 거 있어요? asks for a different item entirely; 다른 색 있어요? specifically asks about color. 다른 색깔도 있나요? is softer/more tentative. Watch 다른 (other) vs 다음 (next) — they are completely different words.
검은색으로 있어요? (in black?), 밝은 색 있어요? (lighter colors?), 무광으로 있어요? (matte finish?). All use the same 있어요? frame with a descriptor.
Hunting for a 'have' verb and saying 다른 색 가져요? — Korean uses 있다 for availability. Confusing 다른 (other) with 다음 (next). Dropping 색 and asking just 다른 거 있어요? loses the color meaning.

mistakes: Looking for a verb 'to have' and saying 다른 색 가져요?
Korean expresses 'have/there is' with 있다, not a possessive verb here. Ask 다른 색 있어요?
Confusing 다른 (other) with 다음 (next).
다른 색 = another color; 다음 색 = 'next color', which makes no sense in a shop. Use 다른.
Dropping 색 and asking only 다른 거 있어요?
That asks for a different item, not specifically a color. Keep 색: 다른 색 있어요?

english: Do you have a bigger one?
usage: Do you have a bigger one?
Polite size request to a clerk
Do you have a smaller one?
examples: 이거 더 큰 거 있어요?
Do you have this in a bigger size?
Bare size request holding an item that feels too small
이 티셔츠 좀 작아요. 더 큰 거 있어요?
This T-shirt is a bit small. Do you have a bigger one?
Stating the problem then the request — the natural order
A: 허리가 좀 끼는데 더 큰 거 있어요? / B: 지금 이 색은 이 사이즈밖에 없어요. / A: 그러면 다른 색으로 볼게요.
A: It's a little tight at the waist — do you have bigger? / B: For this color we only have this size. / A: Then I'll check another color.
Real fitting scenario showing a common clerk response; 끼다 = to feel tight; 사이즈밖에 = only this size
nuance: 더 큰 거 있어요? is a customer asking for a larger size or larger item; 더 means 'more', 큰 is 크다 ('big') in its noun-modifying form, 거 is the spoken 것 ('thing/one'), and 있어요? means 'do you have?', so literally 'is there a more-big one?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 더 큰 거 있어?, softer 더 큰 거 있나요?. The axis runs: 더 큰 거 ↔ 더 작은 거; you can also say 더 큰 사이즈 있어요? using the loanword 사이즈. The nearest vaguer alternative, 다른 사이즈 있어요? ('do you have another size?'), doesn't specify direction; 더 큰 거 is unambiguous about which way. The critical grammar error is 크는 거 — descriptive adjectives (형용사) use the -ㄴ/은 modifier form before nouns, not the -는 of action verbs; 큰 거 is correct, 크는 거 is wrong. Also note 거 is spoken; in formal writing it is 것.

structuredNuance.t: 더 = 'more' + 큰 = adjective modifier form of 크다 'big' + 거 = spoken 것 'one/thing' + 있어요? = 'is there?'. Literally 'is there a more-big one?' Korean stacks the comparator 더 before the adjective, not a separate comparative suffix like English '-er'.
해요체 — after trying on clothing or footwear that is too small. The same structure works for any comparison: 더 밝은 거 (brighter), 더 저렴한 거 (cheaper). Casual 더 큰 거 있어? with a friend.
다른 사이즈 있어요? is vaguer — it doesn't say which direction. 한 치수 큰 거 있어요? ('one size up') is even more precise. 더 큰 거 is the clearest general way to indicate you need bigger.
더 작은 거 있어요? (smaller), 한 치수 큰 거 있어요? (one size up), 더 큰 사이즈 있나요? (softened). Swap 큰 for any adjective: 더 긴 거, 더 가벼운 거.

Saying 크는 거 instead of 큰 거 — descriptive adjectives use -ㄴ, not -는 (which is for action verbs). Also 거 is spoken; write 것 in formal contexts. Don't omit 더: bare 큰 거 있어요? just asks 'is there a big one?' not specifically 'bigger than this'.

mistakes: Saying 크는 거 instead of 큰 거.
크다 is a descriptive adjective; before a noun it takes -ㄴ: 큰 거. -는 is for action verbs, so 크는 거 is wrong.
Using 거 in formal writing.
거 is the spoken contraction of 것. In speech 더 큰 거 is natural; in writing use 더 큰 것.
Mixing up 크다 (big) and 작다 (small).
더 큰 거 = bigger; 더 작은 거 = smaller. Pick the right adjective for the direction you want.

usage: Softer, 중 = in the middle of, with -ㄴ가요
Using 할인 instead of the loanword 세일
examples: 이거 세일해요?
Is this on sale?
Bare question pointing at a tagged item in a clothing or department store
A: 이거 세일해요? / B: 네, 30% 할인이에요. / A: 잘됐다, 살게요.
A: Is this on sale? / B: Yes, it's 30% off. / A: Great, I'll take it.
Complete exchange showing how the question naturally leads to a purchase decision
이 코너 전부 세일해요? 아니면 이것만요?
Is this whole section on sale, or just this one?
Real floor-browsing situation; 코너 = section; 이것만 = just this one
nuance: 이거 세일해요? is a customer checking whether an item is currently discounted; 세일 is the English loanword 'sale' used as a noun, and 하다 makes it a verb ('to be on sale'), so 'does this do a sale?'. This is the go-to word in department stores and franchises — the opposite context from 깎아 주세요 at a market, where pricing is negotiated in person. Politeness is 해요체; casual 세일해?; softer 세일 중인가요?. The native synonym is 할인 (割引), heard more in formal announcements, on receipts, and in corporate settings; 세일 is the breezy everyday spoken word. The dividing line: 세일 = colloquial, spoken, used by shoppers; 할인 = formal, written, used in store policy. English speakers mistakenly say 온 세일이에요? ('on sale') copying English syntax, but Korean treats 세일 as a 하다-verb. Also critical: Korean 세일 only means 'discounted'; 'available for purchase' is entirely different — 이거 파는 거예요? ('is this for sale?').

structuredNuance.t: 세일 (loanword 'sale') + 해요? (do you do?). Literally 'does this do a sale?' Korean attaches 하다 to the noun 세일 to make a verb — you don't need an extra 'on' preposition. The question checks for a discounted price, not store availability.

해요체 — use in department stores, branded franchises, and clothing chains where items are sometimes marked down. Not applicable at traditional markets where you just haggle (깎아 주세요). Casual 세일해? with a friend.

할인해요? / 할인되는 거예요? are native Sino-Korean equivalents, slightly more formal and written-register. 세일 is the everyday shopper's word; 할인 is the word on official signs and receipts. Both mean 'discounted'.
세일 중인가요? (mid-sale?), 몇 퍼센트 할인돼요? (what percent off?), 행사 중인가요? (is there a promotion?). Use 행사 for broader promotions beyond simple price cuts.
Saying 온 세일이에요? copies English 'on sale' — Korean uses 세일하다 as a verb: 세일해요?. Confusing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (purchasable) — 세일 = discounted only; availability is 이거 파는 거예요?

mistakes: Saying 온 세일이에요? copying English 'on sale'.
Korean uses 세일 as a 하다-verb. Ask 이거 세일해요? — there is no 'on' construction.
Mixing 'on sale' (discounted) with 'for sale' (available).
세일 = discounted only. To ask if something is purchasable, say 이거 파는 거예요?, not 세일.
Treating 세일 and 할인 as different deals.
They mean the same; 할인 is just more formal/written. Either 세일해요? or 할인돼요? works.

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar staff
examples: 이거 환불돼요?
Can I get a refund on this?
Bare question holding the item and receipt — check policy before assuming yes
A: 사이즈가 안 맞아서요, 환불돼요? / B: 네, 영수증 있으세요? / A: 네, 여기요.
A: It doesn't fit, so can I get a refund? / B: Yes, do you have the receipt? / A: Yes, here it is.
Realistic refund desk exchange; 안 맞다 = doesn't fit — shows the typical receipt check
어제 샀는데 한 번도 안 썼어요. 영수증도 있고요. 환불돼요?
I bought it yesterday and never used it. I have the receipt too. Can I refund it?
Full real case building the best argument for a refund; 한 번도 안 = not even once
nuance: 환불돼요? asks a clerk whether a refund — getting money back — is possible; 환불 is Sino-Korean 還拂 (return + pay), and 되다 means 'to be possible/doable', so 'is a refund doable here?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 환불돼?; formal 환불 가능한가요?. You ask 환불돼요? to find out the policy, and 환불해 주세요 to actually demand it. The defining contrast in Korean retail is 환불 (refund — money back) vs 교환 (exchange — swap for a different item): these are handled by different counters and have different policies, and English 'return' blurs them; you must decide which you want before walking up. A very practical Korean reality: many shops require the original receipt (영수증), unused tags, and the item in original packaging — without these, even valid refund policy may be refused. Spelling trap: 돼요 not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼).

structuredNuance.t: 환불 = Sino-Korean 還拂 'return-pay' + 되다 = 'to be possible'. Literally 'is a return-of-payment possible?' 되다 is the Korean workhorse for 'can/may something happen here?', not a specific 'refund' verb.

해요체 — say to a clerk at a return/exchange counter or to the same cashier if same-day. Always bring the 영수증 (receipt) and keep original tags. 환불 가능한가요? is a notch more formal for department store customer service.

교환돼요? (can I exchange?) is the all-important alternative — 환불 = money back, 교환 = swap for another item. Never use the English loanword 리펀드; no Korean shopper uses it. After confirming refund is possible, say 환불해 주세요 to execute it.
환불 가능한가요? (more formal), 환불해 주세요 (please refund me), 환불 정책이 어떻게 돼요? (what is the refund policy?). The last is useful for online purchases.
English 'return' blurs 환불 and 교환 — decide which you want. Spelling: 돼요 not 되요. Loanword 리펀드 is never used in Korean shops.

mistakes: Writing 환불되요.
되다's polite form is 돼요 (되+어요). The correct spelling is 환불돼요?
Confusing 환불 (refund) with 교환 (exchange).
환불 = money back; 교환 = swap for another item. Say the one you mean — they are handled differently.
Using the loanword 리펀드.
Korean uses 환불, not a transliteration of 'refund'. Ask 환불돼요?

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar staff
I'd like to exchange it for another
Stating what you want to swap to
examples: 이거 교환돼요?
Can I exchange this?
Bare question holding the item — check policy before assuming yes
사이즈가 작아서요, 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요?
It's small, so can I exchange it for a bigger one?
Reason plus target size; 걸로 = 것으로 (for the one) — the 으로 particle marks what you're swapping to
A: 색이 화면이랑 달라서요. 다른 색으로 교환돼요? / B: 네, 영수증이랑 택 있으시면요. / A: 둘 다 있어요.
A: The color's different from the screen. Can I exchange it for another color? / B: Yes, if you have the receipt and tags. / A: I have both.
Online-purchase exchange scene; 화면 = screen; 택 = product tag — shows typical conditions
nuance: 교환돼요? asks whether you can swap an item for a different size, color, or model without getting money back; 교환 is Sino-Korean 交換 ('mutual exchange') and 되다 = 'to be possible', so 'is an exchange doable?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 교환돼?; formal 교환 가능한가요?. The defining contrast remains 교환 (swap item, keep the transaction) vs 환불 (cancel transaction, get money back); knowing which you want before approaching the counter saves time. To specify what you're exchanging to, use TARGET + 으로/로 교환: 더 큰 걸로 교환돼요?, 다른 색으로 교환돼요? — the directional particle 으로/로 is essential and often dropped by English speakers. After confirming the policy, say 교환해 주세요 to actually execute it. Spelling: 교환돼요, not 교환되요.

structuredNuance.t: 교환 = Sino-Korean 交換 'mutual exchange' + 되다 = 'to be possible'. Literally 'is an exchange possible?' Unlike 환불 (money back), 교환 swaps the item while keeping the original transaction — no refund is involved.

해요체 — use at a return/exchange counter. After getting permission, say 교환해 주세요 to execute it. Bring the receipt (영수증) and keep tags attached — many shops refuse without them. 교환 가능한가요? for formal customer service calls.

환불돼요? = money back; 교환돼요? = item swap. English 'change it' tempts the verb 바꿔요? (바꾸다), which works casually (바꿀 수 있어요?) but the official store word on signs is 교환. Always pair with 으로/로 to name the target item.
다른 색으로 교환돼요? (exchange for another color), 더 큰 걸로 교환해 주세요 (exchange for a bigger one please), 교환 및 환불 가능한가요? (are exchanges and refunds possible? — formal query).
Dropping the 으로/로 particle — Korean marks the target of an exchange with 으로/로, not zero. Saying 교환되요 — correct spelling is 교환돼요. Using 바꿔요? casually instead of the store-official 교환.

mistakes: Writing 교환되요.
되다's polite form is 돼요. Correct: 교환돼요?
Dropping the particle: 다른 색 교환돼요?
You swap INTO something, marked with 으로/로. Say 다른 색으로 교환돼요?
Confusing 교환 (exchange) with 환불 (refund).
교환 swaps the item; 환불 returns your money. Ask for the one you actually want.

usage: 반말 to a friend, rare to staff
Could you give me the receipt?
examples: 영수증 주세요.
Please give me the receipt.
Bare request as you pay — the default at any checkout
영수증 주세요. 혹시 교환할 수도 있어서요.
Please give me the receipt. In case I might exchange it.
Reason for keeping it; 혹시 = just in case — shows why receipts matter in Korean retail
A: 카드로 계산할게요. 영수증 주세요. / B: 현금영수증도 해 드릴까요? / A: 네, 010으로 해 주세요.
A: I'll pay by card. Please give me the receipt. / B: Shall I also do a cash receipt (tax)? / A: Yes, please register it to my 010 number.
Full real checkout; 현금영수증 = tax-deductible cash receipt tied to your phone number
nuance: 영수증 주세요 is a customer asking the cashier for the receipt after paying; 영수증 is Sino-Korean 領收證 (receive + collect + proof), meaning 'proof of payment', and 주세요 is the polite 'please give me'. Politeness is 해요체; softer 영수증 좀 주시겠어요?. A key Korean reality: many stores ask 영수증 드릴까요? and the receipt is your only leverage for refunds or exchanges, so keeping it is important. Do not confuse 영수증 (standard purchase receipt) with 현금영수증 (a separate tax-deductible receipt registered to your phone number or tax ID — completely different and actively solicited at the counter). The phrase also pairs with 주세요 naturally with no particle needed, though 영수증을 주세요 is also correct and slightly more formal. Common pronunciation error: 영수정 — the final syllable is 증, from 證 'proof', not 정.

structuredNuance.t: 영수증 = Sino-Korean 領收證 'proof of receiving payment' + 주세요 = 'please give me'. Literally 'please give me the proof of payment.' 주세요 already means 'give me', so no 저에게 or 에게 is needed.
해요체 — say to any cashier right after paying. The cashier may ask first: 영수증 드릴까요? Answer 네, 주세요 to get it or 아니요, 괜찮아요 to decline. Soften to 좀 주시겠어요? at a formal counter.

현금영수증 is NOT the same as 영수증 — it is a tax-deductible receipt registered to your phone number, used for year-end tax deductions. Ask for it separately: 현금영수증도 해 주세요. 영수증 버려 주세요 is the eco-decline option.
영수증 좀 주시겠어요? (softer), 영수증 있어야 교환돼요? (do I need the receipt to exchange?), 현금영수증도 해 주세요 (and a tax receipt please). In Korean retail these two receipts serve different purposes.
Mispronouncing/spelling it as 영수정 — the final syllable is 증 (證), not 정. Adding 저에게 — 주세요 already means 'give me'. Confusing 영수증 with 현금영수증, which is a separate tax registration.

mistakes: Confusing 영수증 with 현금영수증.
영수증 = the purchase receipt; 현금영수증 = a tax cash-receipt tied to your number. Different things; ask for the one you need.
Adding 저에게: 저에게 영수증 주세요.
주세요 already means 'give me'. Just say 영수증 주세요 — the 'to me' is built in.
Misspelling it 영수정.
The correct word is 영수증 (證, 'proof'). Get the final 증 right.

usage: Polite reply to a hovering clerk
examples: 그냥 둘러볼게요.
I'm just looking around.
Bare reply when a clerk asks if you need help — the standard browse-and-decline phrase
A: 뭐 찾으세요? / B: 아, 괜찮아요. 그냥 둘러볼게요.
A: Can I help you find something? / B: Oh, it's okay. I'm just browsing.
Complete clerk-customer exchange showing the natural trigger for this phrase; 뭐 찾으세요? = 'what are you looking for?'
도움 필요하시면 부를게요. 일단 그냥 둘러볼게요.
I'll call you if I need help. For now I'm just looking.
Shows the speaker proactively managing the clerk; 일단 = for now; 부를게요 = I'll call you — friendly and considerate
nuance: 그냥 둘러볼게요 is the customer's polite brush-off to a clerk who offers help: it signals 'no thanks, just browsing, no pressure needed'; 그냥 means 'just/for no particular reason', 둘러보다 is 'to look around/browse (a space)', and -ㄹ게요 expresses the speaker's intention ('I'll...'), making it gracious rather than dismissive. Politeness is 해요체; casual 그냥 둘러볼게. An equally common equivalent is 구경 좀 할게요 (구경 = 'looking around for pleasure/sightseeing'), which sounds slightly lighter and friendlier. The -ㄹ게요 ending is crucial: it signals personal intention from the speaker's side, which fits perfectly for declining unsolicited help; swapping to -아요 (둘러봐요) makes it a flat factual statement, losing the gracious 'I'll...' nuance. English speakers often say 그냥 보고 있어요 ('I'm just watching/looking'), which is understandable but flat; 그냥 둘러볼게요 is the idiomatically correct browsing phrase. Spelling: 둘러볼게요, not 둘러볼께요.

structuredNuance.t: 그냥 = 'just/for no particular reason' + 둘러보다 = 'to look around' + -ㄹ게요 = 'I will (for my part)'. Literally 'I'll just look around.' The -ㄹ게요 ending is what makes it a gracious intention, not a flat statement.

해요체 — say to any clerk who approaches you offering help. Triggered by 뭐 찾으세요? or 도와드릴까요?. Casual 그냥 둘러볼게 with a friend. You can soften further with 네, 좀 볼게요 (just a brief look) or extend courtesy by adding 도움 필요하면 부를게요 (I'll call if I need help).
구경 좀 할게요 is a near-twin using 구경 (leisurely looking), which sounds slightly lighter and friendlier. 그냥 보고 있어요 is flat and factual — it lacks the courteous 'intention' nuance of -ㄹ게요.
그냥 구경 좀 할게요 (I'll just browse), 잠깐 둘러볼게요 (I'll look around briefly), 나중에 필요하면 부를게요 (I'll call if I need you later). All use the same -ㄹ게요 intention frame.
Saying 그냥 보고 있어요 — natural but flat, not the idiom. Using 둘러봐요 (statement) instead of 둘러볼게요 (intention). Spelling: 둘러볼게요 not 둘러볼께요 (tense pronunciation but 게 spelling).

mistakes: Saying 그냥 보고 있어요 for 'just looking'.
That literally means 'I'm just watching' and feels flat. The natural browse-and-decline phrase is 그냥 둘러볼게요 or 구경 좀 할게요.
Using 둘러봐요 instead of 둘러볼게요.
둘러봐요 is a flat statement; -ㄹ게요 adds the polite 'I'll...' intention that fits declining help. Use 둘러볼게요.
Spelling it 둘러볼께요.
Although pronounced tense (께), the correct spelling of the -ㄹ게요 ending is 게: 둘러볼게요.

usage: Same decision, asking to be handed it
examples: 이걸로 할게요.
I'll take this one.
Bare decision, pointing at your choice — the moment you commit to a purchase
A: 고민했는데 이걸로 할게요. / B: 포장해 드릴까요? / A: 아니요, 그냥 봉투만 주세요.
A: I thought it over — I'll take this one. / B: Shall I wrap it? / A: No, just a bag is fine.
Complete purchase decision → wrap/bag choice; shows realistic follow-up from the clerk
둘 다 예쁜데 이걸로 할게요. 이거 하나만 주세요.
Both are pretty, but I'll take this one. Just this one, please.
Choosing between two options; 하나만 = just one — a very realistic browsing-to-buying moment
nuance: 이걸로 할게요 is how a customer announces their final purchase decision to a clerk; 이걸로 is the spoken contraction of 이것으로 ('with/by means of this one'), and 하다 here means 'to go with / decide on', plus -ㄹ게요 'I'll...', so the whole meaning is 'I'll go with this one'. The particle 으로/로 is doing the selection work: Korean marks the chosen option with 으로/로, not with the object particle 을/를, which is why it must be 이걸로 and not 이걸 or 이것을. Politeness is 해요체; casual 이걸로 할게; formal 이걸로 하겠습니다. The near-twin 이걸로 주세요 is interchangeable at checkout: 할게요 foregrounds your decision/commitment, 주세요 foregrounds the request to hand it over. The -ㄹ게요 ending once again signals personal intention, perfectly suited to committing to a purchase. Spelling: 할게요, not 할께요.

structuredNuance.t: 이걸로 = 이것으로 (with/by this one) + 하다 = 'to go with/decide on' + -ㄹ게요 = 'I will...'. Literally 'I will go with this one.' 하다 here is not 'do' in the activity sense but a decision verb meaning 'to choose/settle on'.

해요체 — say to any clerk when you've made your final choice. Signals you are done browsing. -ㄹ게요 communicates personal commitment, which is exactly right for a purchase. Follow with 계산해 주세요 (please ring it up) to move to checkout.

이걸로 주세요 is interchangeable — it shifts the frame from 'I decide' to 'please hand me this'. 이거 살게요 ('I'll buy this one') is also natural but more casual and explicit about buying. The particle 으로 is non-negotiable for selection.
그걸로 할게요 (I'll go with that one), 저걸로 할게요 (that one over there), 이걸로 두 개 주세요 (two of this one please). Swap the demonstrative to point at different items.
Using the object particle: 이것을 할게요 — selection takes 으로/로, not 을/를. Dropping 로 and saying 이거 할게요 sounds slightly off. Spelling: 할게요 not 할께요.

mistakes: Saying 이것을 할게요 with the object particle.
Choosing an option uses 으로/로, not 을/를. The natural form is 이걸로 할게요 (이것으로).
Dropping the 로 and saying 이거 할게요.
Selection is marked with 으로/로. 이걸로 할게요 sounds complete; bare 이거 할게요 is a bit off.
Spelling it 할께요.
Despite the tense pronunciation, the -ㄹ게요 ending is spelled 게: 할게요.

english: Please wrap it up / pack it
examples: 이거 포장해 주세요.
Please wrap this up.
Bare request handing the item to staff — use in any shop selling giftable goods
A: 선물할 거라서요, 예쁘게 포장해 주세요. / B: 리본도 달아 드릴까요? / A: 네, 부탁드려요.
A: It's a gift, so please wrap it nicely. / B: Shall I add a ribbon? / A: Yes please.
Realistic gift-wrap exchange; 예쁘게 = prettily; 리본 = ribbon — shows how to extend the request
따로따로 포장해 주세요. 선물 세 개예요. 같은 종이로 해 주세요.
Please wrap them separately. It's three gifts. Use the same wrapping paper for all.
Detailed multi-gift request; 따로따로 = each separately; 같은 종이로 = with the same paper
nuance: 포장해 주세요 asks staff to wrap or pack an item, said by a customer; 포장 is Sino-Korean 包裝 ('wrapping/packaging'), 하다 makes it a verb, and -아 주세요 means 'please do it for me'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 포장해 줘; softer 포장 좀 해 주시겠어요?. Crucially, 포장 has two distinct meanings: in a shop it means gift/parcel wrapping; in a restaurant or café it means 'takeout/to-go' (포장이요 = 'to take away'), the opposite of 먹고 갈게요 ('I'll eat here'). Context always determines which meaning applies. For gifts, specify 선물 포장 ('gift wrap') to signal you want decorative wrapping, not just a bag. The -아/어 주세요 frame is a workhorse pattern for service requests, and you can stack adverbs before it: 예쁘게 포장해 주세요, 따로따로 포장해 주세요. English speakers reach for 싸다/싸 주세요 ('to wrap/bundle'), which is also 싸다 'cheap' — confusing; the clean, unambiguous word is 포장. Never drop 주세요 and say 포장해요 — that is a flat statement, not a request.

structuredNuance.t: 포장 = Sino-Korean 包裝 'wrapping/packaging' + 해 주세요 = 'please do for me'. Literally 'please do wrapping for me.' The -아/어 주세요 frame transforms any verb into a service request.
해요체 — use in any shop selling giftable goods (cosmetics, clothes, stationery, food gifts). Casual 포장해 줘 with a friend. Soften to 포장 좀 해 주시겠어요? in upscale boutiques. Stack 예쁘게/따로따로/같이 to specify how.

선물 포장 돼요? ('can you gift-wrap?') checks whether the option exists before requesting. 싸 주세요 exists but is informal and confusable with 싸다 'cheap'. In restaurants 포장이요 = 'takeout' — the same word, opposite context.
예쁘게 포장해 주세요 (wrap it nicely), 따로 포장해 주세요 (wrap them separately), 선물 포장으로 해 주세요 (please do gift wrapping). Any adverb before 포장해 주세요 customizes the request.
Dropping 주세요: 포장해요 sounds like 'it wraps', not a request. Using 싸 주세요 for gift-wrapping when 싸다 also means 'cheap'. Remember 포장 means 'takeout' in restaurants — context decides.

mistakes: Saying 포장해요 without 주세요.
포장해요 is a flat statement ('it wraps / wraps it'). To request, use the -아 주세요 frame: 포장해 주세요.
Using 싸 주세요 for store gift-wrapping.
싸다 works but is informal and overlaps with 싸다 'cheap'. The clear word for wrapping is 포장: 포장해 주세요.
Forgetting 포장 also means 'takeout' in restaurants.
In a café/restaurant 포장이요 means 'to go'. For wrapping a purchased item it means gift/parcel wrapping — context decides.

usage: 반말 to a friend or familiar vendor
Fuller, slightly more formal with 결제
examples: 카드 돼요?
Do you take card?
Bare question at a small stall or food truck before ordering — the essential market survival phrase
A: 카드 돼요? / B: 아니요, 현금만 받아요. / A: 아, 그러면 근처에 ATM 있어요?
A: Do you take card? / B: No, cash only. / A: Oh, is there an ATM nearby?
Realistic small-vendor exchange showing the common 'cash only' outcome and the natural follow-up
카드 돼요? 만 원 이하도 카드 괜찮아요?
Do you take card? Is card okay even under 10,000 won?
Real small-shop worry; 이하 = or less — some vendors require a minimum for card
nuance: 카드 돼요? is the essential question before buying at any small vendor — markets, street stalls, small restaurants, and food trucks where card acceptance is not guaranteed; 카드 is the loanword 'card' and 되다 means 'to work/be possible', so 'does card work here?'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 카드 돼?; fuller and more formal 카드 결제 되나요? (결제 = 'payment/settlement'). The contrast pair is 카드 (card) vs 현금 (cash); the flip question is 현금만 받아요? ('cash only?'). Korean registered businesses are legally required to accept cards, so the question mainly matters for informal street vendors and small unlicensed stalls. Spelling: 돼요, not 되요 (되 + 어 = 돼). English speakers build 신용카드를 받아요? ('do you receive credit card?'), which is grammatical but stiff and over-literal — the native compact form uses 되다 for possibility: 카드 돼요?

structuredNuance.t: 카드 (loanword 'card') + 돼요? (되다 = 'is it possible/does it work?'). Literally 'does card work (here)?'. 되다 is the Korean way to ask if something is accepted or possible — more idiomatic than 받다 ('to receive').

해요체 — ask before ordering or picking an item at small stalls, markets, food trucks, and independent restaurants. In Korean chain stores, department stores, and supermarkets card is universally accepted; this question is for informal vendors. Casual 카드 돼? with a friend.
카드 결제 되나요? is slightly more formal and complete. 현금만 받아요? ('cash only?') flips the polarity — useful when you expect refusal. 체크카드도 돼요? ('does debit work too?') if you want to specify card type.
삼성페이 돼요? (Samsung Pay accepted?), 카카오페이 돼요? (Kakao Pay?), 외국 카드 돼요? (foreign card?). All follow the X 돼요? pattern for payment methods.
Saying 신용카드를 받아요? — grammatical but stiff. 카드 돼요? is the compact, idiomatic native form. Spelling: 돼요, not 되요 (되+어=돼).

mistakes: Writing 카드 되요?
되다's polite form is 돼요 (되+어). Ask 카드 돼요?
Saying 신용카드를 받아요? as the default.
It's grammatical but stiff. The natural everyday question uses 되다: 카드 돼요?
Assuming everywhere is cash-only like some countries.
In Korea registered shops must accept cards; cash-only is mainly street stalls. Still, 카드 돼요? is the right check.

examples: 봉투 주세요.
Please give me a bag.
Bare request as items are being rung up — necessary since bags are not automatically given
봉투 주세요. 종이봉투로요.
A bag, please. A paper one.
Specifying type; 종이봉투 = paper bag; 비닐봉투 = plastic bag — both cost extra in most shops
A: 봉투 하나 주세요. 얼마예요? / B: 비닐이요, 이십 원이에요. / A: 주세요.
A: One bag please. How much? / B: Plastic, twenty won. / A: I'll take it.
Realistic cashier exchange; 비닐봉투 = plastic bag with a small fee — shows the normal checkout script
nuance: 봉투 주세요 asks the cashier for a shopping bag at checkout; 봉투 means 'bag/envelope' and in a retail context always refers to a carry bag; 주세요 is 'please give me'. Politeness is 해요체; casual 봉투 줘; softer 봉투 하나 주시겠어요?. A critical Korean reality: since 2019 plastic bags (비닐봉투) are no longer free in most retail stores — the cashier may ask 봉투 드릴까요? ('shall I give you a bag?') and there will be a small charge. Paper bags (종이봉투) are also often sold separately. The eco-decline is 봉투 필요 없어요 ('no bag needed'). Do not confuse 봉투 (a checkout carry bag) with 가방 (a handbag, backpack, or travel bag you own) — saying 가방 주세요 would mean 'give me a handbag'. English speakers also reach for the loanword 백 (bag), but 백 in Korean implies a fashion bag; the checkout word is 봉투. And 주세요 already means 'give me', so 저에게 is redundant.

structuredNuance.t: 봉투 = 'bag/envelope' (in retail = carry bag) + 주세요 = 'please give me'. Literally 'please give me a bag.' 봉투 in a shop context always means a checkout carry bag, not a handbag or envelope.

해요체 — say to the cashier right before or as they begin bagging your items. Since 2019 most Korean retailers charge for plastic bags; expect a small fee. Soften to 봉투 하나 주시겠어요? for extra politeness. Declining: 봉투 필요 없어요.

가방 주세요 would mean 'give me a handbag' — completely wrong at checkout. 백 (loanword 'bag') sounds like a fashion bag. 쇼핑백 is a loanword that works but is less natural than 봉투 at a cashier. 봉투 is the only natural choice.
종이봉투 주세요 (paper bag please), 큰 봉투로 주세요 (a big bag please), 봉투 두 개 주세요 (two bags please), 봉투 필요 없어요 (no bag needed). Specify material or size with the adjective before 봉투.
Saying 백 주세요 for a shopping bag — 백 = fashion bag. Confusing 봉투 (carry bag) with 가방 (personal bag/purse). Adding 저에게 — 주세요 already means 'give me'.

mistakes: Confusing 봉투 with 가방.
봉투 = a shopping/carry bag or envelope; 가방 = a handbag/backpack you own. Ask 봉투 주세요 for a checkout bag.
Using the loanword 백 for a shopping bag.
백 suggests a fashion bag. The word for a carry bag at checkout is 봉투: 봉투 주세요.
Assuming bags are free.
Korean shops charge for 비닐봉투 (plastic). You may be asked 봉투 드릴까요? — expect a small fee.
